levels.title: Fan Out
levels.story: Rowan unrolls a map of seven clearings joined by trails. "One cabin, one waterfall, lots of paths," says Rowan. "Which way first?" Kit grins. "All of them, a little at a time."

everyday.scene: When you lose a key at home, you check the nearest places first, then the places a little further away. That ring-by-ring habit has a name in planning.
everyday.question: How can a program explore every route without getting lost?
everyday.answer: It keeps a to-do list of places to visit next. Always taking the oldest entry makes it explore in widening rings, which is called breadth-first search.

lessons.title: Places and moves
text: Planning turns into searching. Each possible situation is a state, drawn as a dot. Each action that turns one state into another is a line between two dots. Searching means walking this map of states, starting at the initial state, until you land on a goal state.
In Kit's wood the states are clearings and the actions are paths. Kit stands at S, the cabin clearing, and the goal is G, the waterfall.

terms.meaning: One possible situation of the world.
Exploring the map of states to find a goal state.

lessons.title: Ring by ring
text: Breadth-first search keeps a queue called the frontier: places seen but not yet explored. It takes the oldest entry, looks at its neighbours, and adds any new ones to the back.

So the search spreads in rings: everything one step away, then everything two steps away, and so on. The first time it reaches the goal, no shorter route exists. On Kit's map it visits S, A, B, C, D, E and then G, and the shortest route is 3 steps: S, B, E, G.

terms.meaning: The places seen but not yet explored.
A list where the oldest entry is taken first.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

lessons.title: Diving deep
text: Depth-first search uses a stack instead: it takes the newest entry, so it follows one trail all the way down before trying another. Its first answer may be longer than the best one.

If it tries neighbours in alphabetical order, it finds the waterfall by S, A, D, E, G: 4 steps, though 3 were possible. Meanwhile the tree of choices grows quickly: with 3 moves per state there are 3, 9, 27, 81 and 243 states at depths 1 to 5.

terms.meaning: A list where the newest entry is taken first.

deeper.title: Why guidance matters
text: Because the number of states grows exponentially with depth, searching blindly gets out of hand even on small problems. The next level adds a guess about distance to cut the work down.

fieldNotes.title: Breadth-first search
fieldNotes.text: Breadth-first search explores all the nodes at the present depth before moving on to the next depth level, using a queue to keep track of what is waiting.

fieldNotes.title: Depth-first search
fieldNotes.text: Depth-first search explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack. It does not generally find shortest paths.

fieldNotes.title: State-space search
fieldNotes.text: In state-space search the states form a graph, and two states are connected if some operation can turn the first into the second.

summary: You treated a planning problem as a map of states, followed the frontier through breadth-first search, and compared it with a depth-first search that dives. You also saw how fast the tree of choices grows.
Rowan squints at the map. "Seven clearings is easy. What if there were a million?" Kit rings the bell. "Then I would want a hint about which way to look."

mistake.title: Thinking the first answer is the best
mistake.text: A depth-first search can stop at the first goal it reaches, which may be a long way round. Breadth-first search checks nearer places first, so its first goal is a shortest one.

levels.title: Guess the Distance
levels.story: A fallen log blocks the straight trail. "Breadth-first looks everywhere," says Rowan. "Try looking where the goal is." Kit holds up a hand with the fingers apart and squints at the waterfall. "About four blocks that way."

everyday.scene: On a bushwalk you glance at the peak and head roughly towards it, instead of exploring every side equally.
everyday.question: How can a program search towards the goal, not all around it?
everyday.answer: It adds a guess of the distance still to go to the distance already walked, and explores the lowest total first. That is A* search.

lessons.title: Walked plus guessed
text: A* gives every frontier cell a score, f = g + h. The number g is the cost already spent to get there. The number h is a guess of the cost still to go. A* always explores the cell with the lowest f.
In Kit's grid, Kit starts at A2 and wants E2. At the start g is 0 and h is 4, so f is 4. Each time Kit steps, g rises by 1.

terms.meaning: The cost of the path so far, from the start to this cell.
A guess of the cost still to go, from this cell to the goal.
g plus h: the score A* uses to choose what to explore.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

lessons.title: Counting blocks
text: On a grid where you can only move along rows and columns, a handy guess is the Manhattan distance: the columns apart plus the rows apart. From B3 to E2 it is 3 + 1 = 4.

The guess ignores obstacles. The log at C2 forces Kit to walk further than the guess says, and that is fine. A guess that is too low only makes A* a little less sure of itself. With this guide A* looked at 7 cells before reaching E2. Breadth-first search had to look at all 14.

predict.prompt: What is the Manhattan distance from A2 to E2?
predict.answer: 4, because the cells are 4 columns apart and in the same row.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

lessons.title: Never promise too much
text: A guess is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to the goal. With an admissible guess, A* returns a cheapest route. A guess that is too big can mislead it.

Picture a path straight from S to G costing 10, and another through M costing 2 + 2 = 4. If the guess says M is 20 from G, then M scores 2 + 20 = 22, and A* takes the cost-10 path. The best route was hidden by the overestimate.

terms.meaning: A guess that is never higher than the real cost still to go.

text.text: A guess of 0 everywhere is admissible too, but it gives no hint, so A* then explores all the cheapest cells first, like a plain cost-ordered search.

fieldNotes.title: A* search
fieldNotes.text: A* picks the path that minimises f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g is the cost so far and h is a heuristic estimate of the cost still to go.

fieldNotes.title: Admissible heuristics
fieldNotes.text: A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal, so it acts as a lower bound.

fieldNotes.title: Manhattan distance
fieldNotes.text: Taxicab or Manhattan distance adds the absolute differences of the coordinates. The name comes from a city with a rectangular grid of streets.

summary: You scored cells with f = g + h, used Manhattan distance as a guess, watched A* look at half as many cells as breadth-first search, and saw how an overestimate can hide the best route.
Rowan taps the log. "A guess that is too bold costs you the best path." Kit nods. "So guess low, but guess well."

mistake.title: Guessing high to be safe
mistake.text: A guess higher than the true cost can make A* skip the best route. A guess that is too low is safe, only less helpful.

levels.title: Never the Same Spot Twice
levels.story: Kit follows a trail and arrives, for the third time, at the same fallen tree. "We are going in circles," says Rowan. "Mark where you have been." Kit ties a ribbon on the trunk.

everyday.scene: In a big shopping centre you can walk past the same fountain again and again. A pocket map with a tick on every place you have visited stops that.
everyday.question: How does a search avoid going round in circles?
everyday.answer: It keeps a list of every state it has seen, and only adds a state to its to-do list the first time it finds it.

lessons.title: Loops waste effort
text: Many states can be reached by more than one route, and some routes loop back. A search that forgets where it has been keeps exploring the same states again.
On a grid where you can step up, down, left or right, there are 4 routes of length 1, 16 of length 2 and 1,024 of length 5. Yet only 61 different cells lie within 5 steps of the start.

head: Steps
Routes of that length
Different cells within that many steps

lessons.title: A reached set
text: The fix is a reached set: a list of every state already seen. When the search finds a neighbour, it adds it to the frontier only if it is not in the reached set yet.

Each state is then explored at most once, so the work depends on the number of states, not the number of routes. On the loop map in the sim, 7 neighbour checks are skipped because the state was already reached.

terms.meaning: Every state the search has already seen.
A state reached again by another route.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

lessons.title: When costs differ
text: When every step costs the same, the first route to a state is a shortest one, so skipping later arrivals is safe. When steps have different costs, a later route might be cheaper.
Then the search remembers the cheapest cost found so far for each state. It adds a state again only when a new route beats that cost.

deeper.title: Both cases in one rule
text: A single rule covers both: add a neighbour if it has never been reached, or if the new route is cheaper than the best one so far.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

fieldNotes.title: Revisiting nodes
fieldNotes.text: Graph traversal may visit some vertices more than once, so it is usually necessary to remember which vertices have already been explored.

fieldNotes.title: Reached set
fieldNotes.text: A common pattern is to keep a frontier of places to explore and a set of places already reached, adding a neighbour only if it has not been reached.

source.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to the A* algorithm

fieldNotes.title: Route planners
fieldNotes.text: A search has to remember which places it has already explored, so that it revisits them as little as possible and cannot go round in circles forever. In planning, the set of states already reached plays that part.

summary: You saw how routes multiply while the number of different states stays small, added a reached set so each state is explored once, and learned the extra rule needed when step costs differ.
Rowan counts the ribbons. "One per clearing, no more." Kit smiles. "And no more circles."

mistake.title: Trusting a search that never checks for repeats
mistake.text: A search with no record of what it has seen can loop forever, or waste time on the same states. A reached set keeps the work to the number of states.
